source: FAO/OIE/World Bank, "Good Practices for Biosecurity in the Pig Sector - Issues and Options in Developing and Transition Countries", FAO Animal Production and Health Paper No. 169, Rome, 2010.
text: Pig pathogens spread through several main routes farmers should be aware of: direct pig-to-pig contact (the most common route, especially in close, prolonged or repeated contact); people (carried on footwear, clothing and hands, and sometimes as symptomless nasal carriers); vehicles and equipment used to move pigs or feed; contaminated feed, water, and especially unboiled food scraps (swill); pig manure and bedding, which can carry parasites and bacteria into soil, water and the human food chain if not managed; and wildlife or pests such as birds, rats, ticks and flies, as well as stray or feral animals. Some pigs that appear healthy can still be 'silent carriers' shedding pathogens, which is why newly acquired pigs should never be assumed safe just because they look well.
